title: DNS Security Introduction and Requirements
subtitle: The overview of how DNS answers get digital signatures, and what those signatures can and cannot promise.
summary: RFC 4033 introduces the DNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC), which add data origin authentication and data integrity to the Domain Name System by attaching digital signatures to DNS data. It defines the vocabulary, explains what DNSSEC does and does not provide, and maps out the companion documents RFC 4034 and RFC 4035 that hold the details. It obsoleted the earlier RFC 2535 design.

eli5.summary: Imagine every answer from the phone book comes with a wax seal that only the real owner can make. You can check the seal to know nobody changed the answer on the way, but the seal does not hide what the answer says.

questions: what is a trust anchor in dns
what is a chain of trust in dnssec
what is the difference between a key signing key and a zone signing key

tldr.problem: Plain DNS answers carry no proof of where they came from, so a forged or tampered answer looks just like a real one.
tldr.mechanism: Zone owners sign their record sets with private keys. Resolvers check those signatures through a chain of public keys that leads back to a configured trust anchor.
tldr.outcome: Resolvers can tell secure, insecure and bogus data apart and can authenticate even a claim that a name does not exist. Confidentiality and protection against denial of service are deliberately not part of it.

today: DNSSEC is deployed on the public DNS. The root zone was signed in 2010, and many top-level domains and a growing number of ordinary domains are signed. Validating recursive resolvers, including the large public ones and widely used resolver software such as BIND and Unbound, check signatures by default or by simple configuration. RFC 4033 is still the base overview, although later documents have updated it (RFC 6840 and RFC 6014).

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document introduces the Domain Name System Security Extensions (DNSSEC). It is the first of a three-document core, together with RFC 4034 and RFC 4035, which update, clarify and refine the security extensions of RFC 2535 and its predecessors. The extensions consist of a set of new resource record types and modifications to the existing DNS protocol in RFC 1035.

The headline promise is stated plainly: the extensions provide origin authentication and integrity protection for DNS data, as well as a means of public key distribution. They do not provide confidentiality.

The set obsoletes RFC 2535, RFC 3008, RFC 3090, RFC 3445, RFC 3655, RFC 3658, RFC 3755, RFC 3757 and RFC 3845, and updates (without obsoleting) RFC 1034, RFC 1035, RFC 2136, RFC 2181, RFC 2308, RFC 3225, RFC 3007, RFC 3597 and the DNSSEC parts of RFC 3226.

This document is an overview and requirements text. The record formats live in RFC 4034, and the changes to resolver and server behavior live in RFC 4035.
sections.eli5: This is the front door to a three-book set about putting wax seals on DNS answers. It tells you what the seals are for and which book has the details.

sections.title: Key terms
sections.content:
Section 2 is a glossary meant to be skimmed first and revisited later. A few terms carry most of the weight.

Authentication chain
An alternating sequence of DNSKEY and DS record sets, each link vouching for the next, ending at a key that signs the data you asked for.
Trust anchor
A configured DNSKEY, or the DS-style hash of one, that a validating resolver uses as the starting point for building a chain.
Key signing key and zone signing key
Two roles for keys. A KSK signs other keys and can live longer. A ZSK signs the zone data and may change often. Validation does not tell them apart, and one key may play both roles.
Island of security
A signed zone with no DS record in its parent, so its keys must be trusted by some means outside DNS.

The section also separates security-aware from security-oblivious software, and defines validating and non-validating stub resolvers, zone apex, delegation point, and signed and unsigned zones.
sections.eli5: Before the story starts, the RFC hands out name tags for everyone: the person who holds the master stamp, the person who checks the seal, and the starting stamp everyone agrees to trust.

sections.title: Services provided
sections.content:
DNSSEC provides data origin authentication, data integrity, and authenticated denial of existence. It does this by adding four record types and two header bits: Resource Record Signature (RRSIG), DNS Public Key (DNSKEY), Delegation Signer (DS) and Next Secure (NSEC); and the Checking Disabled (CD) and Authenticated Data (AD) bits. It also requires EDNS0 for the larger messages, and the DO (DNSSEC OK) bit so that a resolver can say it wants the DNSSEC records.

Signatures are attached to whole RRsets and stored in RRSIG records. An important point is that the signing key belongs to the zone, not to the zone's name servers. A resolver learns the zone's public key from a configured trust anchor or from a DNSKEY record that is itself signed. Parent zones vouch for child keys with DS records, so the usual chain is DNSKEY, then zero or more DS to DNSKEY steps, then the signed RRset. A resolver normally builds it from the root downward, though local policy has the last word.

For negative answers, NSEC records link each existing name to the next in a canonical order, describing the gaps and listing the types present, so "no such name" or "no such type" can be signed too.
sections.eli5: Every answer gets a seal. The owner of each neighborhood is vouched for by the owner of the city above it, all the way up to a seal you already trust. Even "nobody lives here" gets a sealed note.

sections.title: What DNSSEC does not provide
sections.content:
DNS was designed on the assumption that every asker gets the same answer and that all its data is visible. So DNSSEC is not designed to provide confidentiality, access control lists, or other ways of treating inquirers differently.

It also gives no protection against denial of service attacks. In fact the RFC warns that signature checking adds a new class of such attacks, because an attacker can try to burn a resolver's or server's cryptographic effort.

Finally, DNSSEC is not meant to protect operations such as zone transfers and dynamic update (RFC 2136, RFC 3007). The RFC points to the transaction-level schemes TSIG (RFC 2845) and SIG(0) (RFC 2931) for those. The distinction is object security versus channel security: DNSSEC signs the data, not the conversation.

Do not read DNSSEC as encryption. Anyone on the path can still read your queries and the answers.
sections.eli5: A wax seal proves a letter was not changed. It does not hide the words, it does not stop someone from stuffing your mailbox, and it does not protect the delivery truck.

sections.title: Scope and the four validation states
sections.content:
The document set is written so that a validating entity can unambiguously decide the state of the data. There are four states.

Secure means the resolver has a trust anchor and a chain of trust and can verify every signature. Insecure means it has a trust anchor and a chain down to a delegation point where signed proof shows there is no DS record, so everything below is provably unsigned. Bogus means the resolver has a trust anchor and a secure delegation showing the data should be signed, but validation fails: missing, expired or unsupported signatures, or data that an NSEC says should exist is missing. Indeterminate means there is no trust anchor covering that part of the tree, which is the default mode.

The last hop is only partly specified. A name server tells a non-validating stub resolver that data is bogus by returning RCODE 2, "Server Failure", and tells a security-aware stub resolver that data is secure with the AD bit. The specification does not define a way to explain why data was bogus, and the signaling does not distinguish indeterminate from insecure. Local policy decides what to accept.
sections.eli5: After checking, an answer gets one of four labels: sealed and good, honestly unsealed, sealed but fake or broken, or "I have no idea who to trust here."

sections.title: Resolvers, zones and name servers
sections.content:
Sections 6 through 9 describe what each role must do differently.

Resolvers. A security-aware resolver must be able to verify signatures with at least the mandatory-to-implement algorithms, build authentication chains, and should be configured with at least one trust anchor. Any security-oblivious proxy or NAT device in between can break DNSSEC, and DS records are especially awkward since they do not follow the usual ownership rules at zone cuts.

Stub resolvers. A non-validating stub resolver must trust its recursive server and the channel to it. That channel needs integrity and authentication but not confidentiality, for example via TSIG, SIG(0) or IPsec. Such a stub may read the AD bit as a hint. A validating stub can set the CD bit and check signatures itself.

Zones. A TTL and a signature validity period are different things. The TTL controls caching, and the RRSIG inception and expiration times bound how long a signature is usable. A signed zone needs regular re-signing, which also means bumping the SOA serial and may trigger NOTIFY and zone transfers.

Name servers. They should include DNSSEC records when the query has the DO bit set, must support the EDNS sender's UDP payload size mechanism because the larger answers can cause truncation and fallback to TCP, and should keep private keys offline where possible. Zones with dynamic update need an online zone signing key, which is one reason to split KSK from ZSK.
sections.eli5: Each helper has a different job. The checker needs a starting stamp to compare against, the person who signs must keep re-signing before the old seals run out, and the server must send the seals along with the answers.

sections.title: The document family
sections.content:
Section 10 sorts DNSSEC documents into four groups under the DNS base protocol.

The DNSSEC protocol document set is the core of three: this introduction, RFC 4034 (Resource Records for DNS Security Extensions) and RFC 4035 (Protocol Modifications for the DNS Security Extensions). The Digital Signature Algorithm Specification set has one document per signature algorithm. The Transaction Authentication Protocol set covers message authentication such as TSIG and is related to, but not part of, DNSSEC. The New Security Uses set covers uses of DNS to store and distribute things such as certificates (RFC 2538), which DNSSEC can support without directly securing them.

The IANA section adds nothing: this overview introduces no new IANA considerations, and RFC 4034 holds the full review.
sections.eli5: The set is like a library shelf with a main trilogy, a shelf of books about each kind of stamp, a shelf about secret handshakes between servers, and a shelf of new uses.

sections.title: Security considerations
sections.content:
The RFC's own limits section is candid. To validate, every zone along the path from the trusted starting point must be signed, and every name server and resolver involved must be security-aware. A break anywhere means the affected data cannot be validated.

A non-validating stub resolver is vulnerable to attacks on, and by, the recursive servers that validate for it and to attacks on the channel to them. Channel security defends against the second; the only known defense against the first is to validate on its own.

DNSSEC does not protect against denial of service and opens a new class based on cryptographic work: an attacker can tamper with RRSIG records or build needlessly complex signature chains, or flood a dynamic-update server so it re-signs more often than necessary. It does not provide confidentiality, "due to a deliberate design choice".

Finally, NSEC chains let a hostile party enumerate all the names in a zone by following the links from name to name. That is not an attack on DNS itself, but it can help map hosts and resources.

Zone walking through NSEC is a known property of this design. Later work (not covered here) addresses it.
sections.eli5: The seals only work if every step of the chain is sealed and everyone checking knows how. Anyone can still jam the system with fake paperwork, and the "nobody lives here" notes can be read one after another to list every house.
